theme: Plagues of frogs, gnats, flies, livestock, and boils
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 8:1-9:35. These chapters contain the plagues of frogs, gnats, flies, the death of livestock, boils, and hail. Do not rush. Look for the phrase “that you may know,” and watch what happens each time Pharaoh seems to give in.
settingTheScene: The plagues are not random disasters. Each one is aimed at something the Egyptians trusted, such as the Nile, the frogs associated with the goddess Heqet, the animals associated with their religion, and the sky. God says that through the plagues he will execute “judgments” on all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12). They are a contest between the LORD and the powers that seemed to rule Egypt. They are also a mercy, because they give Pharaoh repeated chances to let Israel go.
observation: Moses says, “Let my people go, that they may serve me” (8:1). The plague of frogs fills the land, and Pharaoh asks Moses to pray to the LORD to remove it (8:8).
When the frogs die, Pharaoh “hardened his heart and would not listen to them” (8:15).
The magicians cannot produce gnats and say to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God” (8:19).
With the flies, God says, “I will set apart the land of Goshen…that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth” (8:22).
The livestock of Egypt die, but not one of the animals of Israel (9:6).
The boils afflict the magicians themselves, so that they “could not stand before Moses” (9:11). “The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh” (9:12).
God says to Pharaoh, “For this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (9:16).
Before the hail, God offers a chance to shelter the servants and livestock. Some Egyptians who feared the word of the LORD brought them in (9:19-21).
Pharaoh says, “I have sinned this time; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong” (9:27), and then he sins again (9:34-35).
interpretation:
There is a pattern in the plagues, and it is worth noticing. Pharaoh is confronted. He stalls, then gives way under pressure, and then goes back on his promise when the pressure is lifted. This is a picture of a heart that is not changed by judgment alone. Frogs, gnats, flies, and boils make him say what he must, but nothing in him changes. This is a warning to every one of us that pain alone does not make a person repent. You need a new heart.

The magicians are a surprising feature of the story. At first they copy Moses’ signs. But with the gnats, they fail and confess, “This is the finger of God.” Even Pharaoh’s own advisers have to admit that something beyond them is at work. And by the sixth plague they cannot even stand. The power of the Egyptian gods is shown to be empty.

God makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel. In the land of Goshen there are no flies, and Israel’s livestock do not die. The plagues are not simple natural disasters. They are directed, and God protects his own. This is the theme of redemption, to which the narrative keeps returning: God sets his people apart.

The most important statement in these chapters comes in 9:16. “For this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.” God’s goal is bigger than freeing Israel. He wants all the world to know who he is. You can see that the exodus is always for the sake of his name, and that this is a good thing. The best thing that could happen to any person is to know the true God.

Then there is the hail. God gives a warning to those who will hear. Some Egyptians, “who feared the word of the LORD,” gather their servants and flocks indoors. This is a small piece of mercy in the middle of judgment: even in Egypt, anyone who trusted God’s word was spared. It is a hint of what the book will say later, that foreigners could join Israel (12:38).

Pharaoh’s confession in 9:27 is the most striking detail. He says all the right words: “I have sinned. The LORD is in the right.” But by verse 34 he is sinning again. A confession without repentance is just speech. Compare it to Psalm 106, where Israel also sang God’s praise and soon forgot.
connection: Revelation 16 describes the bowls of judgment in language drawn from these plagues. Romans 9:17 quotes Exodus 9:16. Jesus said that “everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48). Jesus also distinguishes true repentance from regret in the parable of the two sons (Matthew 21:28-32) and in Paul’s words about “godly grief” in 2 Corinthians 7:10.
application:
Ask yourself if there is a pattern in your life of making promises to God under pressure and forgetting them afterward. Bring it to him honestly.

If you are tempted to think that God’s judgments are arbitrary, notice how patient he is in these chapters. He gives repeated warnings and offers shelter.

Remember that God sets his people apart. Thank him for the ways he has marked you as his own.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for his patience with those who resist him, and for the mercy in his warnings.
Ask him for a heart that truly repents, not just a mouth that says so.
Thank him for setting his people apart.
